video_title: How to Invest for A Hundred Years | Inigo Fraser Jenkins
gist: Alliance Bernstein chief investment strategist Inigo Fraser Jenkins lays out his '100-year portfolio' framework: strip away the recency bias of the post-1980 benign-inflation era and the post-WWII rules-based order, replace market/60-40 benchmarks with purchasing-power preservation, redefine risk as the probability of real loss over multi-decade holding periods, and redefine diversification as robustness across divergent futures (AI, climate, geopolitics) rather than low historical correlation. The public episode covers only the first hour (framework); the allocation building blocks and macro discussion sit behind the paywall.

insights.claim: Inigo Fraser Jenkins argues long-horizon investors must strip out two layers of recency bias: the post-1980 regime of benign inflation, high growth and negative stock-bond correlation, and the longer post-WWII US-led rules-based order, both of which no longer apply in the same way.
insights.speaker: Inigo Fraser Jenkins
insights.so_what: Portfolio assumptions calibrated on 1980-2020 data (bond hedging, low inflation, high real returns on low-risk assets) should be stress-tested against a regime where none of these hold.

insights.claim: Fraser Jenkins identifies AI, climate change and geopolitical breakdown of the rules-based order as forces that genuinely widen the range of possible future paths beyond the usual 'the future is always uncertain' caveat, making long-run forecasting unusually hard today.
insights.speaker: Inigo Fraser Jenkins
insights.so_what: Wider dispersion of outcomes argues for scenario-robust portfolios over point-forecast optimization.

insights.claim: Historically, periods in which low-risk assets reliably delivered positive real returns were exceptions (post-1980, the post-war growth era, and the late-19th-century Pax Britannica); outside those regimes investing was much more turbulent, so assuming the current regime persists is a bet, not a baseline.
insights.speaker: Inigo Fraser Jenkins
insights.so_what: Investors comfortable relying on bonds for real returns are implicitly making a regime call that history suggests is fragile.

insights.claim: Since the 1970s financial assets have hugely outperformed real-world assets, an unusual pattern historically, driven in part by financialization and levering up: government balance-sheet leverage and corporate buybacks shrinking share counts both inflated asset prices.
insights.speaker: Inigo Fraser Jenkins
insights.so_what: If leverage-driven multiple expansion cannot repeat, forward returns from financial assets will rely more on real growth and inflation pass-through.

insights.claim: Fraser Jenkins views most asset classes as fully valued or expensive on a cross-asset basis, but frames this as not a bearish call; rather, valuations give little ability to make claims about returns beyond the near horizon.
insights.speaker: Inigo Fraser Jenkins
insights.so_what: Expect a lower-return future without an explicit timing signal; plan for real-return shortfalls rather than a crash.
insights.quote: in a cross asset perspective most asset classes are fully valued/ maybe expensive that doesn't mean it should be interpreted as a bearish statement

insights.claim: Fraser Jenkins holds that finance and social science are not sciences with universal laws, and that treating empirical regularities as laws is especially dangerous during regime change.
insights.speaker: Inigo Fraser Jenkins
insights.so_what: Models and rules of thumb formed over a career should be held with humility when the macro regime shifts.
insights.quote: I certainly take the view that finance and social science in general is not a science.

insights.claim: Return drivers differ by horizon: under one year, technicals, momentum and flows dominate; around ten years, valuation and mean reversion matter most; over multi-generational horizons valuation matters less and real growth rates and the probability of preserving purchasing power become critical.
insights.speaker: Inigo Fraser Jenkins
insights.so_what: Match the signal to the horizon: a very-long-horizon allocator should weight real growth and inflation pass-through over current valuation spreads.

insights.claim: A short-horizon investor hedging inflation needs assets that correlate with inflation (commodities, TIPS), whereas a long-horizon investor should instead care about the probability an asset delivers a real return through an extended period of elevated, volatile inflation, which can favor equities or farmland despite no short-term inflation correlation.
insights.speaker: Inigo Fraser Jenkins
insights.so_what: Long-horizon inflation protection can come from real-growth assets rather than expensive short-term inflation hedges.
insights.quote: If you worry about inflation but you have a longer horizon, I would argue you don't actually care about the correlation of assets with inflation per se.

insights.claim: Measured over 20-year holding periods, the volatility of stocks and bonds is essentially equal, and beyond a few business cycles the probability of a real loss on bonds exceeds the probability of a real loss on equities.
insights.speaker: Inigo Fraser Jenkins
insights.so_what: For true long-horizon capital, bonds are not the 'low-risk' asset in real terms; this supports an equity-heavy allocation.
insights.quote: the probability of a real loss on bonds becomes greater than the probability of real loss on equities once you extend out beyond a few business cycles

insights.claim: Fraser Jenkins rejects the idea that a long horizon is simply a concatenation of short horizons, because some investment techniques only work over long horizons, though delegating them creates agency problems.
insights.speaker: Inigo Fraser Jenkins
insights.so_what: Long-horizon capital can harvest premia (illiquidity, value) that short-evaluated managers cannot, if governance tolerates the wait.

insights.claim: Fraser Jenkins argues long-horizon portfolios should replace market-based cross-asset benchmarks with purchasing-power preservation, e.g. a real-return target or a probability of not losing money in real terms over a set number of years.
insights.speaker: Inigo Fraser Jenkins
insights.so_what: Shifts allocation toward real assets and away from nominal bonds; measures success against inflation rather than peers or indices.

insights.claim: There is no theoretical basis for a 60/40 portfolio as a natural cross-asset benchmark; it is only empirically validated by having done well over the last 40-50 years.
insights.speaker: Inigo Fraser Jenkins
insights.so_what: Allocators anchored to 60/40 are relying on a regime-specific result; risk-based or inflation-targeting approaches are the suggested alternative.
insights.quote: 6040 is often the default allocation people use but it happens to have done well in the last 40 or 50 years but there's no theoretical basis for it

insights.claim: Alliance Bernstein research found the number of equity indices worldwide measured in the millions against roughly 45,000 listed stocks, which Fraser Jenkins cites as evidence the industry is over-obsessed with benchmarks.
insights.speaker: Inigo Fraser Jenkins
insights.so_what: Benchmark proliferation signals index-centric thinking that can obscure the real objective of outpacing inflation.

insights.claim: The equity market is the biggest real asset because companies can pass inflation through prices and dividends, but parts of equity returns (issuance vs. buybacks, corporate leverage) are financial rather than real activities.
insights.speaker: Inigo Fraser Jenkins
insights.so_what: Favor equities with genuine pricing power over those whose returns come from financial engineering; nominal bonds are the clearest non-real asset.
insights.quote: I say in the note that the equity market is the biggest real asset out there

insights.claim: Within equities, healthcare growth stocks with a long record of raising prices at or above inflation count as real, while an upward shock in discount rates favors short-duration value stocks, and energy/commodity-linked companies have dividend streams tied to an exogenous real asset.
insights.speaker: Inigo Fraser Jenkins
insights.so_what: Screen for inflation pass-through within equities; tilt to value/energy when discount-rate shocks are the risk.

insights.claim: The shift since 2022 to a positive stock-bond correlation is a return to normal: over the roughly 200 years before the last 30, the correlation was positive most of the time.
insights.speaker: Inigo Fraser Jenkins
insights.so_what: Bonds should not be relied on as the default equity hedge; government bonds warrant a diminished role in long-horizon portfolios.
insights.quote: I would argue that that shift since 22 to the correlation asset classes being positive is firstly a return to normality.

insights.claim: Positive stock-bond correlation is consistent with a world of non-growth-linked inflation shocks from climate, deglobalization, or debt monetization, which Fraser Jenkins expects to persist.
insights.speaker: Inigo Fraser Jenkins
insights.so_what: Supply-side inflation regimes erode the bond hedge; diversifiers must work in inflationary drawdowns (gold, real assets).

insights.claim: Fraser Jenkins redefines diversification for multigenerational portfolios as robustness across divergent future paths (e.g. >2°C warming, geopolitical change, an unexpected AI shock to job creation) rather than low correlation among assets in a Markowitz framework.
insights.speaker: Inigo Fraser Jenkins
insights.so_what: Build portfolios via scenario stress tests across plausible worlds rather than optimizing on historical covariance matrices.

insights.claim: A total portfolio approach, which denies the primacy of asset classes and allocates risk by underlying factors across public and private holdings, allocates risk more efficiently when diversification is hard to achieve, but requires a slow, humble governance overhaul that large organizations find difficult.
insights.speaker: Inigo Fraser Jenkins
insights.so_what: Expect more sovereign funds and family offices to migrate to total portfolio approach structures, changing how they size private versus public allocations.

insights.claim: For multigenerational portfolios governance has primacy over any single allocation decision, since it sets the return target, the definition of risk, tolerance for illiquidity, and the horizon over which delegated managers are judged.
insights.speaker: Inigo Fraser Jenkins
insights.so_what: Manager evaluation windows should match the strategy: short for cross-asset momentum, years for value-driven processes.

insights.claim: Payout or spending requirements should be fixed ex ante and not allowed to drift upward after 5-10 years of good returns; avoiding becoming a forced seller is the key liquidity rule for a 100-year portfolio.
insights.speaker: Inigo Fraser Jenkins
insights.so_what: Pro-cyclical spending creep is a major wealth destroyer; hard spending rules preserve the ability to hold through drawdowns.

insights.claim: Holding back extra liquidity for opportunistic buying only pays if the investor will actually deploy it into dislocated single assets or asset classes; otherwise it is a cash drag and the portfolio should be closer to fully invested.
insights.speaker: Inigo Fraser Jenkins
insights.so_what: Size dry powder to realistic behavior, not aspirational opportunism.

insights.claim: Given a lower-return future and high government debt-to-GDP, Fraser Jenkins expects tax rates to rise across many countries regardless of what current politicians say, making tax planning a larger share of taxable investors' take-home returns.
insights.speaker: Inigo Fraser Jenkins
insights.so_what: Tax-efficient structures and location decisions become more valuable alpha sources for taxable long-horizon capital.
insights.quote: whatever the current crop of politicians say across many countries, my view is tax rates are going up, you know, at some horizon.

insights.claim: Inflation is identified as the critical long-run destroyer of wealth today, more so than in the pre-WWI era of dynastic wealth, alongside punitive taxes and social dislocation, the last of which is very hard to diversify against.
insights.speaker: Inigo Fraser Jenkins
insights.so_what: Real-return generation must be the core design constraint for dynastic capital.

insights.claim: Vehicles with genuinely multigenerational horizons (family offices, endowments, sovereign wealth funds) hold only about high-single-digit percent of global assets at best, but their share is growing, amplified by pensions shifting from defined benefit to defined contribution and from nominal to real-asset concerns.
insights.speaker: Inigo Fraser Jenkins
insights.so_what: A rising share of capital oriented to real returns over long horizons supports structural demand for equities and real assets over nominal bonds.

insights.claim: Historical multigenerational portfolios of families and endowments were dominated by real estate, so their lessons transfer only partly to today's financialized portfolios, the main carry-over being the importance of real returns.
insights.speaker: Inigo Fraser Jenkins
insights.so_what: Supports a continued role for direct real estate in dynastic portfolios.

insights.claim: US corporate profit share is as high as it has been in decades and may rise further near term without voter pushback so far, but Fraser Jenkins believes there must be a limit to both profit share and inequality, citing Luke Kemp's 'Goliath's Curse' finding that rising inequality is the key predictor of societal collapse.
insights.speaker: Inigo Fraser Jenkins
insights.so_what: Record US margins, a pillar of US equity exceptionalism, carry political mean-reversion risk; an AI backlash could be the trigger.

insights.claim: Fraser Jenkins argues the current AI path, in which jobs are at risk while a small group becomes much richer, is a social and political choice rather than inherent to the technology, and sees early signs of backlash against AI.
insights.speaker: Inigo Fraser Jenkins
insights.so_what: Policy risk (redistribution, regulation) for AI beneficiaries could rise as social acceptance erodes.
insights.quote: I don't think there's anything inherent in AI that means it has to be that way
